IndusTech Corporation - Q3 2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the IndusTech Corporation Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are in listen-only mode. After the presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To ask a question, you will need to press star one on your touchtone phone. To withdraw your question, press star two. Please limit yourself to one question and one follow-up. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Sarah Jenkins, VP of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Jenkins (VP of Investor Relations):
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss IndusTech Corporation's results for the third quarter of 2024. Joining me on today's call are Michael Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer; David Thompson, Chief Financial Officer; and Lisa Chen, Chief Operating Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking in nature and subject to certain risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Michael Reynolds.

Michael Reynolds (CEO):
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on IndusTech Corporation's performance for the third quarter. We've made significant progress on several fronts, and I'd like to highlight a few key achievements. First, our automation and digital offerings have seen explosive growth, driving efficiency gains across our operations and customer base. Second, demand trends in our core end markets—construction, mining, agriculture, and manufacturing—remain robust, with orders surging and backlog expanding. Third, our cost reduction initiatives under the Efficiency 2.0 program have delivered substantial savings, bolstering profitability. Fourth, total revenue hit a strong milestone with double-digit growth. And fifth, our guidance assumptions reflect confidence in continued economic resilience and end-market strength.

We are confident that our strategic initiatives are positioning us for long-term sustainable growth.

Now, I'll turn the call over to David Thompson to provide more detail on our financial results.

David Thompson (CFO):
Thank you, Michael. Good afternoon, everyone. I'll dive right into our top-line results, which continue to reflect the resilience and strategic positioning of IndusTech in a dynamic industrial landscape.

For the third quarter, total revenue reached $2.82 billion, marking a robust 14.2% increase year-over-year from $2.47 billion in Q3 2023. On an organic basis, excluding the $85 million contribution from our recent acquisition of Nordson Robotics' precision welding division, growth was still an impressive 12.8%. This performance exceeded our guidance midpoint and underscores the strength across our core segments: original equipment manufacturing, aftermarket parts and services, and our growing digital solutions portfolio.

OEM revenue, which includes our heavy-duty CNC machining centers, automated assembly lines, and hydraulic press systems, came in at $1.65 billion, up 16.5% year-over-year. Volume growth of 11% was driven by strong demand from key end-markets like semiconductor fabrication and electric vehicle battery production. Average selling prices rose 4.8% due to favorable pricing discipline amid steel and aluminum cost pass-throughs, as well as premium features like our IndusLink IoT platform for predictive maintenance. Notably, bookings in OEM hit a record $1.92 billion, pushing our backlog to $8.7 billion—up 22% year-over-year—fueled by multi-year contracts with players like TSMC for advanced wafer fab tools and Ford for next-gen stamping lines.

Aftermarket and services revenue grew 11.8% to $1.02 billion, representing 36% of total sales—a key margin-accretive mix shift. This was propelled by higher utilization rates in our installed base, now exceeding 85% globally, thanks to our Equipment-as-a-Service model rollout. Remanufactured components for legacy fleets, such as our PowerForge hydraulic cylinders akin to those in large dozers, saw 19% growth, while service contracts tied to Industry 4.0 upgrades—like AI-driven vibration analytics—added $180 million in recurring revenue.

Regionally, North America led with 18.3% year-over-year growth to $1.48 billion, benefiting from the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act tailwinds in data center construction and reshoring of steel mills. EMEA delivered 12.1% growth to $720 million, supported by wind turbine OEM demand from Siemens Gamesa and Vestas, despite softer auto sector exposure in Germany. Asia-Pacific, at 8.7% growth to $620 million, faced headwinds from China's property sector slowdown but was bolstered by a 25% surge in Indian capex for solar panel assembly lines and electronics manufacturing services from Foxconn.

These results validate our Smart Factory 2030 initiative, where we've invested $450 million year-to-date in R&D for electrified and modular equipment platforms. For instance, our new IndusEV series of battery gigapress machines—competing head-to-head with IDRA's offerings—secured 15% market share in EV structural casting within 18 months of launch, capturing share from incumbents like Buhler. Sustainability trends are also paying off: 42% of Q3 OEM shipments met our net-zero steel sourcing standards, appealing to ESG-focused customers like Tesla's supply chain.

That said, we navigated challenges like lingering supply chain constraints on rare earth magnets for servo motors and inflationary pressures on forgings, which compressed gross margins by 120 basis points to 38.4%. Our proactive hedging and vertical integration—now 65% of components in-house—mitigated much of this.

Gross margin was 38.4%, driven by pricing actions, mix shift toward high-margin digital offerings, and cost efficiencies. Operating expenses were $650 million, resulting in an operating income of $420 million. Our net income for the quarter was $320 million, or $1.42 per share.

Turning now to demand trends across our key end markets—construction, mining, agriculture, and manufacturing—which collectively represent about 92% of our fiscal Q3 revenue, up from 89% a year ago as we continue to optimize our portfolio toward high-margin OEM equipment and aftermarket parts. Overall, we saw a robust 14% year-over-year increase in orders across these segments, with our book-to-bill ratio expanding to 1.28x from 1.15x last quarter, driven by a $2.7 billion backlog that's now up 22% sequentially. This reflects healthy capex cycles and replacement demand amid elevated utilization rates averaging 85-90% globally for our core products like hydraulic excavators, wheel loaders, and dozers.

Starting with construction, which accounted for 38% of Q3 revenue, delivering 16% organic growth. North American demand remains a bright spot, fueled by the IIJA, where federal funding has accelerated highway and bridge projects—we've seen a 25% surge in orders for our 20-40 ton-class excavators from contractors like Kiewit and Fluor. Housing starts ticked up modestly to 1.42 million annualized units per Census Bureau data, supporting our mid-sized backhoe loaders, but non-residential construction is the real driver, with data center builds for hyperscalers like AWS and Google pushing demand for rough-terrain forklifts and telehandlers. In EMEA, trends are mixed: UK and German infrastructure spending is solid at €150 billion annually, but softening residential activity amid high interest rates has tempered orders by 5% year-over-year; we're countering this with our new Tier 4 Final compliant electric mini-excavators, which saw 40% adoption in urban rental fleets like Loxam. Asia-Pacific is accelerating, with India's $1.4 trillion National Infrastructure Pipeline driving a 30% order increase for our rigid-frame dump trucks, while China's Belt and Road projects in Southeast Asia bolstered volumes. Strategically, we're investing $150 million in telematics upgrades across our GPS-enabled site optimization systems, which have improved fleet productivity by 15% for customers, enhancing our aftermarket attach rates to 28% of sales.

Shifting to mining, our second-largest market at 28% of revenue, up 18% year-over-year with exceptional strength in ultra-class haul trucks and autonomous solutions. Commodity tailwinds are clear: copper prices hovering at $4.50 per pound and iron ore above $120/tonne have spurred capex, with global mining equipment demand projected at $145 billion for 2024 per off-highway research from firms like RK Dynamics. In Australia, our Pilbara operations customers like Rio Tinto and BHP have ramped ultra-class 400-tonne trucks, contributing to a 35% backlog build in rigid haulers; our Command for Hauling autonomy tech is now deployed on 250 units, delivering 20% uptime gains and reducing OPEX by 12%. North America saw Permian Basin oil sands activity boost shovel and drill rig orders by 22%, while Latin America's copper belt—Chile and Peru—grew 25%, though permitting delays capped upside. Electrification is a key initiative: our battery-electric hauler prototypes are in field trials with Freeport-McMoRan, targeting 30% lower emissions by 2026, aligning with ESG mandates. Regionally, Africa's artisanal mining rebound added 10% to volumes, but we're selective, focusing on Tier 1 assets. Our strategy here emphasizes service contracts, now 35% of mining revenue, leveraging predictive maintenance via our IndusLink IoT platform to capture 95% retention rates.

In agriculture, representing 15% of revenue, demand grew 12% year-over-year, but with some lumpiness tied to commodity prices and weather. US farm incomes are projected at $128 billion for 2024 per USDA, supporting a healthy equipment replacement cycle—tractors over 100 HP saw 15% order growth, particularly our autonomous row-crop models with See & Spray tech. Precision agriculture adoption hit 55% in North America, driving demand for our GPS-guided sprayers and yield monitors, which boosted precision ag revenue by 28%. Brazil's soybean harvest, despite La Niña risks, fueled a 20% surge in high-horsepower tractors for customers like SLC Agricola, with our 400HP+ 4WD units filling the void left by delayed deliveries. EMEA faced headwinds from EU fertilizer subsidies waning, softening demand by 8% in France and Germany, but our variable-rate applicators gained traction in sustainable farming initiatives. Asia's rice and palm oil sectors added modest growth. Key technical push: our FarmSight platform integrates AI for 25% fuel savings, and we're allocating $80 million to hydrogen fuel cell prototypes for large combines by 2027. Outlook is cautiously optimistic, with aging fleets—average tractor age now 14 years—underpinning mid-teens growth.

Finally, manufacturing, at 11% of revenue, rebounded sharply with 20% growth, propelled by reshoring and automation. US onshoring under the CHIPS Act and IRA has ignited factory expansions—orders for our CNC machining centers and industrial robots jumped 30%, serving OEMs like Tesla's Gigafactory ramps and Intel's Ohio fab. Book-to-bill here is 1.45x, with a $450 million backlog in material handling like automated guided vehicles. In China, export restrictions spurred domestic automation, lifting our servo-driven presses by 18%, while Europe's Industry 4.0 push—think Siemens and Bosch—drove collaborative robot arms. Regional note: Mexico's nearshoring boom added 25% to volumes via maquiladoras. Initiatives include our EdgeControl IIoT for real-time OEE improvements, hitting 92% utilization for customers, and strategic partnerships like our JV with Fanuc for cobot integrations. Aftermarket parts here grew 22%, capitalizing on supply chain resilience.

These markets underscore a bifurcated but positive outlook: cyclical strength in mining and construction offsets softer ag pockets, with manufacturing as an emerging growth engine. We're responding with $500 million in capex for capacity at our Peoria and Monterrey plants, targeting 10% output growth, plus $200 million in R&D for net-zero equipment by 2030. Pricing discipline held at 5-7% across segments, margins expanded 220 basis points to 24.8%. We see FY24 end-market growth of 12-15%, with Q4 orders accelerating.

I'll now turn to our cost reduction initiatives, which have been a cornerstone of our strategy to drive sustainable profitability in this challenging macroeconomic environment for the industrial equipment sector. The industry has faced persistent headwinds—steel prices fluctuating 15-20% year-over-year amid supply chain volatility, aluminum costs up 8% due to energy constraints in Europe, and labor inflation averaging 4-6% globally. Labor shortages in skilled trades like welders and CNC machinists have exacerbated this, with U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data showing a 12% vacancy rate in manufacturing roles last quarter.

Despite these pressures, our disciplined Efficiency 2.0 program—launched in Q2 2023—delivered $78 million in run-rate savings for the full year, exceeding our initial $60 million target by 30%. This represented a 4.2% reduction in our total cost of goods sold, directly contributing to a 220 basis point expansion in gross margins from 24.8% in Q4 2022 to 27.0% in Q4 2023. On an adjusted EBITDA basis, these efforts boosted our margins by 310 basis points to 15.4%, helping us outperform peers like Caterpillar and Deere, whose EBITDA margins hovered around 13-14% amid similar commodity pressures.

Supply chain and procurement optimization accounted for 45% of our savings, or $35 million. We've aggressively diversified away from single-source dependencies, particularly in Asia-Pacific, where U.S. tariffs on Chinese steel and components—now at 25% under Section 301—have added 5-7% to landed costs. By consolidating our supplier base from 1,200 to 850 vendors and nearshoring 25% of our forging and casting needs to Mexico and Eastern Europe, we reduced logistics costs by 18%. For instance, our hydraulic cylinder production for excavators and skid steers saw input costs drop 12% through long-term contracts with Mexican foundries like Nemak, hedging against LME steel futures that spiked to $800/ton in Q3. Regionally, this was most impactful in North America, where 60% of savings materialized, shielding us from Red Sea disruptions that inflated ocean freight rates by 40%. In EMEA, energy surcharges on aluminum extrusions for our conveyor systems added headwinds, but strategic stockpiling and alternative sourcing from Turkey mitigated a potential 3% COGS hit.

Manufacturing productivity enhancements drove 30% of savings, or $23 million, through our Industry 4.0 digital transformation. We've deployed over 1,200 IoT-enabled sensors across our 12 global plants, integrated with our SAP S/4HANA ERP platform, enabling predictive maintenance that reduced unplanned downtime by 28%—from 8% OEE losses to under 6%. A flagship initiative was the rollout of 150 collaborative robots from Universal Robots and Fanuc at our Ohio and Monterrey facilities, automating weld seam inspections and palletizing for our material handling equipment. This cut direct labor costs by 15% in those lines, with ROI achieved in 14 months versus the industry average of 24. We also implemented AI-driven yield optimization on our powder coating lines for structural steel frames, improving first-pass yield from 92% to 97.5% and slashing scrap rates by 22%, saving $4.2 million in raw materials alone. In APAC, where our Suzhou plant serves ASEAN markets, these digital twins reduced cycle times by 19% on assembly of pump skids for oil & gas, countering wage inflation of 7% in China. Europe lagged slightly at 20% of regional savings due to higher CapEx hurdles from elevated borrowing costs, but our German facility's adoption of Siemens MindSphere for machine learning-based anomaly detection has positioned us for 25% further gains in 2024.

Overhead and SG&A rationalization contributed 25% of savings, or $20 million. We rationalized our footprint by idling a low-utilization plant in Brazil—now at 55% capacity amid soft LATAM demand for mining equipment—and consolidated back-office functions into shared service centers in India and Poland, trimming headcount by 8% through attrition and voluntary programs, avoiding severance charges. This included migrating to cloud-based PLM software from PTC Windchill, reducing IT spend by 22%. We also optimized our aftermarket service model, a high-margin segment at 35% EBITDA, by expanding predictive analytics via telematics on our fleet of 50,000+ installed units—think condition monitoring for bearings in our rotary hammers and gearboxes. This preempted 15% more failures, boosting parts utilization and extending service intervals by 12%, which flowed through to a 150 bps SG&A deleveraging.

Strategically, these initiatives are embedded in our Resilient Growth Framework, aligning with megatrends like U.S. reshoring under the CHIPS Act and IRA incentives. We're targeting $120-140 million in additional savings for 2024, with 40% from scaling digital tools and 30% from value engineering—e.g., redesigning our 48V electric actuators for forklifts to use 20% less rare earth magnets, tailored to industrial durability standards. The profitability impact has been profound: sequential COGS as a percentage of revenue fell from 75.2% in Q1 2023 to 73.0% in Q4, with adjusted EPS expanding 18% year-over-year to $1.42. Free cash flow conversion improved to 95% of EBITDA, funding $250 million in buybacks and a 10% dividend hike. Risks remain—potential steel price rebounds or union negotiations in the U.S. Rust Belt—but our hedging covers 70% of 2024 exposures, and multi-year labor pacts lock in 3% annual increases.

Efficiency 2.0 has fortified our competitive moat, delivering double-digit returns on invested capital above our 12% WACC hurdle. We're outperforming the sector's median ROIC of 9%, positioning IndusTech for mid-teens EBITDA margins by year-end 2025 as capex cycles inflect.

Good afternoon, everyone. Today, I'd like to dive deep into one of our brightest growth engines: our Automation and Digital Solutions segment, which continues to outperform amid a challenging macro environment in the Manufacturing and Industrial Equipment sector. As you know, this segment—encompassing our programmable logic controllers, supervisory control and data acquisition systems, industrial IoT platforms, robotics, and our flagship IndusEdge AI-driven analytics suite—represented 28% of total revenue in Q3, up from 22% a year ago. Let me break this down with specifics on growth drivers, efficiency impacts, regional dynamics, and our strategic roadmap.

On growth momentum: The segment delivered 32% year-over-year revenue growth to $1.2 billion in Q3, accelerating from 25% in Q2. This was fueled by a 45% surge in digital offerings, including software-as-a-service subscriptions and data analytics, which now account for 42% of segment revenue—more than double the industry average of 20%, per recent Gartner data. Recurring annual contract value from our IndusCloud platform hit $450 million, up 38% year-over-year, with net retention rates exceeding 115% thanks to upsell opportunities in predictive maintenance and digital twins. Hardware sales, like our next-gen EtherCAT-enabled PACs and collaborative robots, grew 22%, supported by pent-up demand post-supply chain bottlenecks. Marginally, this segment expanded to 29.5% operating margins—520 basis points ahead of our core equipment business—driven by 65% gross margins on software versus 38% on traditional hardware.

Turning to impact on efficiency, our solutions are delivering measurable ROI for customers, which in turn bolsters our stickiness and pricing power. Clients deploying our full IndusTech Automation Stack—integrating PLCs, edge gateways, and AI/ML algorithms—saw average OEE improvements of 18% within the first year, based on a sample of 250 deployments tracked via our telemetry data. Downtime reductions averaged 32%, with unplanned outages dropping from 5% to 3.4% through predictive analytics that flag anomalies 72 hours in advance using vibration, temperature, and throughput sensors. This mirrors results from peers like Rockwell Automation's FactoryTalk suite, but our edge computing reduces latency by 40% compared to cloud-only rivals.

A prime example is our partnership with a leading North American automotive OEM, where we retrofitted 15 assembly lines with our cobot swarm technology and IndusEdge digital twins. This yielded a 25% throughput boost and $12 million in annual labor savings—equivalent to a 2.8x ROI in under 18 months. On the sustainability front, energy efficiency gains of 22% per line align with ESG mandates, helping clients cut Scope 2 emissions by 15% while complying with EU CBAM tariffs.

Regionally, performance was robust across the board, reflecting divergent industrial cycles. In the Americas (52% of segment sales), growth hit 35% year-over-year, propelled by U.S. reshoring trends—think the CHIPS Act and IRA incentives driving $50 billion in new fab investments. We've captured 15% market share in semiconductor automation, outpacing ABB, with wins at three new Intel and TSMC facilities. EMEA (28% of sales) grew 28%, buoyed by Germany's Industrie 4.0 push and UK manufacturing renaissance; our SCADA integrations helped a Siemens-partnered wind turbine maker reduce cycle times by 20%. Challenges persist from energy costs, but our efficiency tools mitigated 10-15% of input inflation for customers. APAC (20% of sales) accelerated to 42% growth, led by China's Made in China 2025 digitization—where we grew 55% via localized PLC variants compliant with GB/T standards—and India's PLI scheme, adding $150 million in pipeline from EV battery plants.

Strategically, we're doubling down on three pillars: (1) AI/ML innovation, with $250 million FY24 CapEx for our next-gen IndusEdge 2.0, featuring generative AI for autonomous optimization—think real-time recipe tuning rivaling Honeywell's Forge. Early pilots show 12% yield improvements in discrete manufacturing. (2) Ecosystem expansion, including co-development with AWS on hybrid edge-cloud IIoT and a JV with Fanuc for advanced cobotics, targeting a $10 billion TAM in warehouse automation amid e-commerce labor shortages. (3) M&A firepower, with $1.5 billion dry powder to acquire bolt-on digital pure-plays, focusing on MES to verticalize our stack.

Looking ahead, we see mid-teens segment growth into FY25, outpacing the 8-10% IDC forecast for global industrial automation, as labor scarcity—e.g., 2.1 million U.S. manufacturing vacancies per BLS—and geopolitical volatility favor our lights-out factories. Risks like chip shortages linger, but our diversified supply base—40% from TSMC alternatives—positions us well.

In summary, automation and digital are not just growth vectors; they're transforming efficiency across the value chain, delivering durable margins and customer lock-in. We're excited about the runway ahead.

Thank you, Michael. Now, turning to our full-year 2024 guidance, we're introducing revenue of $8.2 to $8.5 billion, with adjusted EPS in the range of $4.85 to $5.15. This represents organic growth of 4% to 7% at the midpoint, reflecting a balanced view of resilient end-market demand tempered by some near-term macro headwinds. Let me walk you through the key assumptions underpinning this outlook, which are grounded in our rigorous bottom-up forecasting process, incorporating customer order books, capex surveys from our ERP systems, and third-party data from sources like S&P Global and the Institute for Supply Management.

On the macro front, we're assuming modest global economic growth of 2.8% GDP in 2024, down slightly from 3.1% in 2023, aligning with IMF and World Bank consensus. This includes U.S. GDP at 2.4%, Eurozone at 1.2%—reflecting ongoing energy transition challenges—and China at 4.9%, where industrial policy support for high-tech manufacturing should offset property sector weakness. Critically, we're baking in global industrial production growth of 2.5% to 3.0%, with PMI readings stabilizing above 50 in key regions. Capacity utilization in the U.S. manufacturing sector is assumed to hold at 78%, supporting steady equipment replacement cycles.

Diving into end-market demand, our guidance assumes a diversified recovery across our core verticals, weighted toward strength in infrastructure and automation. In non-residential construction and infrastructure—about 35% of our mix—we expect 5% to 6% demand growth, driven by U.S. IIJA funding disbursements exceeding $100 billion annually and similar tailwinds from the EU's NextGenerationEU plan. For context, U.S. highway and bridge capex is projected to rise 8% year-over-year, boosting demand for our hydraulic excavators and asphalt pavers.

Agriculture and mining, representing 25% of revenue, are assumed flat to up 2%, with farm income pressures capping tractor and combine orders—but offset by copper and iron ore prices holding 10% above troughs, spurring $50 billion in global greenfield mine development. We're particularly optimistic on autonomous haul trucks, where our IoT-enabled fleet management system has secured 15% share gains in Australia and Latin America.

Aerospace and defense, now 20% of the portfolio post our 2023 integration, drives the upside with 12% growth assumed, fueled by Boeing and Airbus production ramps to 60+ monthly widebodies and U.S. DoD budgets up 5%. Our electro-hydraulic actuators for the 737 MAX and A320neo are fully tooled, with book-to-bill at 1.4x.

Industrial automation and general manufacturing—30% of mix—sees 4% growth, anchored by reshoring trends under the CHIPS Act and IRA. Factory expansions for semis and EVs will pull through demand for our CNC machining centers and collaborative robots, where we've embedded edge AI for predictive maintenance, reducing downtime by 25% in beta trials.

Regionally, North America is the growth engine at 6% organic, benefiting from pent-up capex and $1.2 trillion in backlog projects. EMEA is muted at 1% to 2%, with German auto OEMs delaying stamping press upgrades amid 7% energy cost inflation, though UK data center builds provide offsets. APAC ex-China grows 5%, led by India's PLI scheme for steel and renewables, while China itself is +3%, with selective exposure to wind turbine nacelles avoiding overcapacity pain points. Latin America rounds out at 4%, buoyed by Petrobras' $10 billion offshore rig program.

Strategically, these assumptions embed pricing discipline—mid-single-digit realization from VAVE initiatives and steel pass-throughs—and 200 bps of gross margin expansion to 28.5% via our Fab40 supply chain resilience program, which localized 60% of castings from Asia. We're also assuming $400 million in R&D deployment toward electrification, with our 48V hydraulic hybrids launching Q3, targeting 20% fuel savings for Class 8 loaders and positioning us ahead of Eaton and Danfoss in the $15 billion e-powertrain pivot.

Of course, these are point estimates with sensitivities: a 1% swing in global IP growth impacts revenue by ~$100 million; commodity volatility, like a 10% steel price drop, hits margins by 50 bps. Upside levers include faster aerospace recovery or tariff protections, while risks center on persistent high interest rates delaying capex or Chinese export deflation.

We're confident this guidance reflects a disciplined, data-driven view, with our 85% visibility from Q4 order intake supporting the trajectory. We are reaffirming our guidance for the full year, with expected revenue growth of 6% at the midpoint and EPS of $4.85 to $5.15. We are committed to returning capital to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases.

Now, I will hand over to Lisa Chen, COO, for an operational update.

Lisa Chen (COO):
Thank you, David. Operationally, we've been focused on streamlining our supply chain and improving manufacturing efficiency. We have implemented several new initiatives that are already yielding positive results, including expansions in automation deployment and digital twins across our plants, which have cut lead times by 15% on average and boosted throughput in high-volume lines like excavator assemblies. We are closely monitoring the global supply chain situation and taking proactive steps to mitigate any potential disruptions, such as dual-sourcing critical components like semiconductors and forgings. We are also investing in automation and digital technologies to enhance our operational capabilities, with over 1,200 new IoT sensors live and cobot integrations scaling to 20% of assembly tasks. These efforts are directly supporting our backlog conversion and positioning us for capacity growth in key markets like North America and India.

Q&A Session:

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question-and-answer session. Our first question comes from John Miller with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Miller (Goldman Sachs):
Good morning. Can you discuss the impact of rising raw material costs on your profitability?

David Thompson:
Thanks for the question, John. Rising raw material costs, particularly steel and aluminum, have been a headwind, with fluctuations of 15-20% year-over-year. However, our Efficiency 2.0 program has more than offset this, delivering $78 million in run-rate savings through supply chain diversification, nearshoring 25% of forgings to Mexico and Eastern Europe, and digital productivity gains like predictive maintenance reducing downtime by 28%. This drove 220 basis points of gross margin expansion to 38.4%, and our hedging covers 70% of 2024 exposures. We're passing through costs where appropriate and see continued margin leverage as these initiatives scale.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Carter with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Emily Carter (JPMorgan):
What is your outlook for demand in the aftermarket services business?

Michael Reynolds:
Good question, Emily. Aftermarket remains a cornerstone, now 36% of revenue up 11.8% year-over-year, driven by high utilization in our installed base and EaaS models. With telematics and predictive analytics on 50,000+ units, we're seeing 95% retention in mining services and 28% attach rates in construction. Demand outlook is strong, with aging fleets and ESG-driven upgrades supporting mid-teens growth into FY25, especially as reshoring boosts replacement cycles.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Robert Hayes with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Robert Hayes (Morgan Stanley):
Can you provide an update on your progress in reducing lead times?

Lisa Chen:
Absolutely, Robert. We've made solid strides, reducing average lead times by 19% quarter-over-quarter through Industry 4.0 investments, including 150 cobots automating palletizing and weld inspections, and AI yield optimization hitting 97.5% first-pass on key lines. IoT sensors across 12 plants cut unplanned downtime to under 6%, and we're on track for another 15-20% reduction in 2024 via digital twins and ERP integrations. This supports our 1.28x book-to-bill and $8.7 billion backlog conversion.

Operator:
Thank you. There are no further questions at this time.

Closing Remarks:

Michael Reynolds:
Thank you for your questions and your interest in IndusTech Corporation. We are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our strategy and delivering long-term value for our shareholders.

Sarah Jenkins:
Thank you, everyone, for joining us today. This concludes our earnings call. Have a great day.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
